title: Engineering Plasmons in Oxide/Graphene Heterostructures via Interfacial Charge Transfer
authors: Yuanchen Chi, Dongxu Di, Michael Fralaide, Jigang Wang, Zhe Fei
abstract: Interfacial charge transfer provides an effective route for tailoring the optical and electronic properties of two-dimensional materials. Here, we investigate infrared surface plasmon polaritons in oxide/graphene heterostructures using scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy. Ultrathin oxide overlayers deposited by physical vapor deposition enable systematic engineering of graphene plasmons through interfacial charge redistribution. MoOx strongly enhances the plasmonic response, producing a longer plasmon wavelength, stronger fringe contrast, and reduced damping, whereas a subsequently deposited ZnOx overlayer partially reverses these changes. Energy-dependent nano-infrared imaging combined with quantitative modeling reveals an increased graphene carrier density and the resulting modification of the plasmon dispersion. Thickness-dependent measurements show a rapid increase in charge-transfer doping at sub-nanometer MoOx thicknesses, followed by a weaker long-range contribution at larger overlayer thicknesses. Electrostatic gating further modulates the carrier density and produces a nonlinear response consistent with gate-dependent interfacial charge redistribution. In addition, an approximately 3-nm-thick MoOx overlayer stabilizes the plasmonic response for at least seven months under ambient conditions. These results establish oxide/graphene heterostructures as a robust platform compatible with scalable fabrication, providing a pathway toward stable and tunable infrared nanophotonic and optoelectronic devices.
summary: This research demonstrates that depositing ultrathin oxide layers on graphene allows for precise engineering of surface plasmon polaritons via interfacial charge transfer doping. By using s-SNOM and quantitative modeling, the authors show that the oxide material dictates the plasmon wavelength and stability, establishing oxide/graphene stacks as a robust platform for tunable infrared optoelectronics.
main_problem: The paper investigates how interfacial charge transfer between oxide and graphene layers can be used to systematically engineer the optical and electronic properties, specifically the surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs), in these heterostructures.
main_result: Depositing $	ext{MoO}_x$ strongly enhances the plasmonic response and increases graphene doping, while subsequent $	ext{ZnO}_x$ deposition partially reverses these effects; the structure proves to be a robust platform for stable nanophotonics.
method: The study combines experimental characterization using scattering-type s-SNOM with quantitative modeling based on multilayer transfer-matrix methods and charge transfer doping models.
model_or_system: The physical system is an oxide/graphene heterostructure (e.g., $	ext{MoO}_x/	ext{graphene}$), where the plasmon dispersion and carrier density are modeled as functions of oxide thickness and external gating voltage.
key_observables: Plasmon wavelength ($\lambda_p$), damping rate ($\gamma_p$), graphene carrier density ($n$), and the evolution of the plasmon dispersion relationship $E(q_p)$.
important_parameters: Oxide layer thickness ($d$), gate voltage ($V_g$), and the work functions of the constituent materials ($\Phi_M, \Phi_Z$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the plasmon field decay using the complex in-plane wavevector, leading to an intensity decay length $L_I = \lambda_p / (4\pi)$.
figures_summary: Figures show nano-IR images comparing bare graphene to structures with $	ext{MoO}_x$ and $	ext{ZnO}_x$, illustrating changes in fringe contrast and wavelength; dispersion plots map the plasmon energy vs. momentum.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents experimental measurements varying oxide thickness and gate voltage, correlating observed plasmon shifts and damping rates with theoretical models of interfacial charge transfer doping and plasmon field decay.
why_interesting: The work provides a clear, tunable mechanism (interfacial charge transfer) to control plasmonic properties in 2D materials, which is highly relevant for designing stable, functional nanophotonic devices.
